'''''Calanthe tankervilleae''''', commonly known as the '''greater swamp-orchid''', '''swamp lily''', '''swamp orchid''',<ref>{{GRIN | accessdate=20 December 2014}}</ref> '''nun's-hood orchid''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PHTA2|taxon=Phaius tankervilleae|accessdate=23 September 2015}}</ref> '''nun's orchid''', '''veiled orchid''', '''Lady Tankerville's swamp orchid'''<ref name="Noosa">{{cite web |title=''Phaius tankervilleae'' |url=https://noosaorchidsociety.org.au/nos/Phaius_tankervilleae.html |publisher=Noosa Orchid Society |accessdate=30 October 2018 |archive-date=30 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181030092347/https://noosaorchidsociety.org.au/nos/Phaius_tankervilleae.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> or '''鹤顶兰 (he ding lan)''',<ref name="China" /> is a species of orchid native to areas from Asia to islands in the Pacific Ocean. It has large, pleated leaves and tall flowering stems bearing up to twenty five white, brown, mauve and yellow flowers. It was named for [[Lady Tankerville]] who was the first person to make the orchid flower successfully in England.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Leatherdale |first=Duncan |date=2023-03-19 |title=Lady Tankerville: The botanist and secret scientist |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-tyne-64938776 |access-date=2023-03-20}}</ref> It was the first tropical orchid to flower in England.

==Description==
''Calanthe tankervilleae'' is an [[evergreen]], [[Terrestrial plant|terrestrial]] [[Herbaceous plant|herb]] that  has cone shaped or more or less spherical [[pseudobulb]]s mostly {{convert|60-80|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|30-60|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide. Between two and eight pleated linear to lance-shaped leaves {{convert|300-1000|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|80-200|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide develop from the pseudobulb. Between ten and twenty five [[Resupination|resupinate]] flowers {{convert|70-125|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide are borne on a flowering stem {{convert|500-2000|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} tall. The flowers are whitish on the outside and reddish brown inside. The [[sepal]]s and petals are oblong to lance-shaped, {{convert|40-65|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|10-15|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide. The [[Labellum (botany)|labellum]] is pink or reddish with a white tip and white stripes inside, {{convert|35-60|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|20-50|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide with three lobes. The middle lobe is more or less tube-shaped and the side lobes have wavy or crinkled edges. There is a whitish yellow spur {{convert|5-10|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long near the base of the labellum and a narrow raised [[Labellum (botany)|callus]] in its centre. Flowering occurs from September to November in Australia and from March to June in Asia.<ref name="Noosa" /><ref name="China">{{cite web |title=''Phaius tencarvilleae'' |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=242424276 |publisher=Flora of China |accessdate=30 October 2018}}</ref><ref name="Bhutan">{{cite web |title=''Phaius tankervilleae'' |url=https://biodiversity.bt/species/show/3911 |publisher=Bhutan Biodiversity Portal |accessdate=30 October 2018}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
In 1778, [[John Fothergill (physician)|John Fothergill]] sent specimens of this orchid back from China to England and in 1788, after one had flowered, [[Joseph Banks]] formally described the species, giving it the name ''Limodorum tankervilleae''. In 2020, [[Mark Wayne Chase]], [[Maarten J. M. Christenhusz]] and [[André Schuiteman]] changed the name to ''Calanthe tankervilleae'' in the journal ''[[Phytotaxa]]''. The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''tankervilleae'') honours [[Charles Bennet, 4th Earl of Tankerville|Lady Emma Tankerville]], as the orchid had flowered in her greenhouse at [[Walton-on-Thames]] near London.<ref name=gift>[https://books.google.com/books?id=dgsfa13J2OIC&dq=%22tankerville%22+orchid+earl&pg=PA88 Gifts from the Gardens of China], By Jane Kilpatrick, {{ISBN|0-7112-2630-X}}, accessed 10 June 2008</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.philipmould.com/catalogue.php?sid=2544&p= |title=Portrait of Emma, Countess of Tankerville (1752-1836) with her daughters Caroline and Anna, Daniel Gardner (C.1750-1805) |accessdate=2010-06-21 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110715074644/http://www.philipmould.com/catalogue.php?sid=2544&p= |archivedate=2011-07-15 }}</ref> It was the first tropical orchid to flower in England.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Lady Tankerville's Legacy: A Historical and Monographic Review of Phaius and Gastrorchis |author-last1=Stone |author-first1=Judi |author-last2=Cribb |author-first2=Phillip |date=2017 |publisher=Natural History Publications |location=Kota Kinabalu, Borneo |isbn=978-983-812-181-1 |url=https://www.nhpborneo.com/book/lady-tankervilles-legacy }}</ref> 

Other spellings of the specific epithet are sometimes used. When [[Charles Louis L'Héritier de Brutelle]] published his book ''Sertum Anglicum'' and cited Joseph Banks' name for this species, he [[Latinisation of names|Latinised]] it to ''Limodorum tancarvilleae''.<ref name="L'Herit.">{{cite book |last1=Héritier de Brutelle |first1=Charles Louis |title=Sertum Anglisum |date=1788 |location=Paris |page=28 |url=http://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/ing/Libro.php?Libro=3544 |accessdate=30 October 2018}}</ref> As a result, some authorities, including the [[Australian Plant Census]], list the species as ''Phaius tancervilleae''.<ref name="China" /><ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Caladenia abbreviata''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/595540|publisher=APNI|accessdate=30 October 2018}}</ref><ref name="Kew">{{cite journal |last1=Mabberley |first1=David J. |title=A note on some adulatory botanical plates distributed by Sir Joseph Banks |journal=Kew Bulletin |date=2011 |volume=66 |issue=3 |pages=465–477|doi=10.1007/s12225-011-9291-y |s2cid=21236279 }}</ref> The spellings ''P. tankervilliae''<ref name="organic">{{cite web |title=Nun orchid care tips:''Phaius tankervilliae'' |url=https://www.gardening-advice.net/nun-orchid.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100820025524/http://www.gardening-advice.net/nun-orchid.html |url-status=usurped |archive-date=August 20, 2010 |publisher=Organic Gardening Advice |accessdate=30 October 2018}}</ref> and ''P. tankarvilliae'' have also been used.<ref name="SOS">{{cite web |last1=Brydie |first1=Jim |title=''Phaius tankervilleae''(?) |url=http://members.iinet.net.au/~emntee/Phaius%20tankervilleae.htm |publisher=Species Orchid Society of Western Australia (Inc.) |accessdate=30 October 2018}}</ref>

In 2017, [[Judi V. Stone|Judi Stone]] and [[Phillip James Cribb]] published a [[monograph]] entitled ''Lady Tankerville's Legacy - A Historical and Monographic Review of Phaius and Gastrorchis'', in which they described six varieties of ''Phaius tankervilleae'':
* [[Phaius tankervilleae var. antoninae|''Phaius tankervilleae'' var. ''antoninae'']] <small>([[Peter Balzer|P.Balzer]]) J.V.Stone & P.J.Cribb (2017)</small>
* [[Phaius tankervilleae var. australis|''Phaius tankervilleae'' var. ''australis'']]<small> ([[F.Muell.]]) J.V.Stone & P.J.Cribb (2017)</small>
* [[Phaius tankervilleae var. baolocensis|''Phaius tankervilleae'' var. ''baolocensis'']]<small> ([[Nong Van Duy|Duy]], [[Tao Chen (botanist)|Tao Chen]] & [[Dian Xiang Zhang|D.X.Zhang]]) J.V.Stone & P.J.Cribb (2017)</small>
* [[Phaius tankervilleae var. bernaysii|''Phaius tankervilleae'' var. ''bernaysii'']]<small> (F.Muell. ex [[Rchb.f.]]) J.V.Stone & P.J.Cribb (2017)</small>
* [[Phaius tankervilleae var. devogelii|''Phaius tankervilleae'' var. ''devogelii'']]<small> J.V.Stone & P.J.Cribb (2017)</small>
* [[Phaius tankervilleae var. tankervilleae|''Phaius tankervilleae'' var. ''tankervilleae'']]

==Distribution and habitat==
''Calanthe tankervilleae'' grows in swampy forest or grassland.<ref name="Noosa"/> It is found in the [[Indian subcontinent]], [[New Guinea]], [[China]], [[Japan]], [[Southeast Asia]], [[Indonesia]], [[Malaysia]], the [[Philippines]], [[Australia]] and certain islands of the [[Pacific]]. It is also naturalised in [[Hawaii]], [[Panama]], the [[West Indies]] and [[Florida]].<ref name="katcher">[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=151105 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families, ''Phaius tankervilleae'' (Banks) Blume]</ref>

In [[Australia]] it is found as [[Phaius tankervilleae var. australis|''P. tankervilleae'' var. ''australis'']] as far south as [[Yamba, New South Wales]].<ref name="Phaius tankervilleae">{{cite web|title=''Phaius tancarvilleae''|work=Australian Native Plants Society|url=http://asgap.org.au/p-tan.html|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080622025340/http://asgap.org.au/p-tan.html|archivedate=2008-06-22}}</ref> and further north in tropical [[Queensland]]. While rare in parts of its native habitat, it is present in other parts of the world as a [[introduced species|naturalised species]], including [[Hawaii]]<ref>USFWS. [http://ecos.fws.gov/docs/five_year_review/doc3302.pdf ''Cyanea remyi'' ''Five-year Review'']. August 2010. pg 4.</ref> and [[Florida]].<ref name=liu>Liu, H. and R. Pemberton. (2010). {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20121216043404/http://article.pubs.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca/ppv/RPViewDoc?issn=1916-2804&volume=88&issue=3&startPage=290|title=Pollination of an invasive orchid, ''Cyrtopodium polyphyllum'' (Orchidaceae), by and invasive oil-collecting bee, ''Centris nitida'', in southern Florida.}} ''Botany'' 88 290-95.</ref>

==Conservation status==
''Phaius tankervilleae'' var. ''australis'', as ''Phaius australis'', is listed as [[endangered]] with possible extinction within the country. It is threatened by trampling by stock, and by illegal collecting, weeds and drainage of its habitat.<ref name="environment">{{cite web |title=Approved conservation advice o ''Phaius australia'' (common swamp orchid) |url=http://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/species/pubs/5872-conservation-advice.pdf |publisher=Australian Government Department of the Environment |accessdate=30 October 2018}}</ref>
